summary: Decide when a part waits for an answer, how messages travel, and how to keep an API safe to change.

items.when: The caller cannot continue without the answer
The work can occur later, or the caller does not care who reacts
Load arrives in bursts
items.use: A queue, so workers process steadily

items.when: Work must be done one time: "convert this video"
Several parts react to one fact: "order placed"
Volume is very high, or a new subscriber must see old events
Related messages must stay in order
items.use: The same key, so the same partition

items.when: Each message is an independent task, and times vary a lot
The user needs a result, but the work takes long
A live screen: chat, delivery tracking
items.use: A push over WebSocket or server-sent events

items.when: Public APIs, web and mobile clients
Calls between internal services, where speed matters
Clients with many different screens
Reactions that do not need an answer
Several services need one address for clients
items.use: An API gateway, with no business rules

items.when: Each kind of client needs data in its own shape
items.use: A backend for frontend (BFF) for each client

items.when: Exact data is essential, such as money to a ledger
Services change at different speeds
items.use: A loose contract, with consumer-driven contract tests

items.text: For a user request, do the minimum that makes the action true, answer, then do the rest in the background.
A chain A to B to C to D, each up 99.9%, is up only about 99.6%.
Long synchronous chains are the most common fault. Join parts that always call each other, or keep a copy.
Asynchronous work needs a "pending" state in the user interface and somebody who watches the queue.
Design for "at least once". Make each receiver safe to repeat.
Name events in the past tense. An "event" named "SendEmail" is a command.
After some attempts, move a message that always fails to a dead-letter list.
A total order over all messages is very expensive and almost never necessary.
The number of partitions limits the parallel work. A hot key makes a hot partition.
Give each queue a maximum size. A queue with no limit hides an overload until the disk is full.
Design the API from the side of the caller. Do not expose your tables.
Accept an idempotency key on each operation that creates or changes something.
Return lists in pages, with a cursor. A list with no limit fails in production.
Errors must tell the caller whose fault it was, and if the caller can try again.
Adding is safe. Removing or renaming a field is not safe.
Changing the meaning of a field is the most dangerous change, because nothing fails visibly.
For a change that is not safe, offer a new version next to the old one. Plan for months.
Hyrum's law: with enough callers, each behavior that they can see becomes a dependency.
Make an unsafe change in safe steps: expand, migrate the callers, then contract.
Be a tolerant reader: ignore unknown fields, but reject data that breaks the rules you use.

blocks.title: Delivery promises
rows: Not a delivery promise: at least once, and the receiver detects repeats

items.when: A public API
items.use: JSON, because reach matters more than size

items.when: Services that you own, inside one organization
items.use: A binary format with a schema

items.when: Schemas are generated, for example from database tables
Data lives a few seconds inside one process
items.use: A language-specific format, such as pickle

items.when: Large integer IDs in JSON
Events on a topic that many services read
items.use: A schema registry that checks each change

items.when: A field must get a new meaning
items.use: A new field with a new name

items.text: Backward compatibility: new code reads old data. Forward compatibility: old code reads new data.
A rolling upgrade needs both directions, because old and new code run at the same time.
Add only optional fields with a default and a new tag. Never add a required field.
Never reuse the tag of a removed field. Reserve it.
A change of meaning, such as grams to kilograms, passes every compatibility check.
Protocol Buffers and Thrift identify a field by its tag. Avro needs the writer's schema to read.
Data outlives code. New code must read old rows for a long time.
The data layer must keep unknown fields. Else old code deletes new data when it writes back.
Never decode language-specific bytes from a source that you do not trust.
A network call can get no answer. Then you do not know if the action ran.
